implementation_notes: The safe default: a one-method Command interface, concrete command classes (or records), and Jackson writing the discriminator with @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, property = "kind") plus an explicit @JsonSubTypes list - the invoker reads the tag, resolves the concrete class and calls execute(). The envelope travels as a JMS TextMessage (Jakarta Messaging), a Kafka/RabbitMQ payload or an HTTP body, so the broker never deserialises Java objects. Blanket default typing must stay off: the per-hierarchy subtype list is the allow-list.
pitfalls: Jackson's global default typing resolves classes named by the payload and is a gadget-chain vector: use per-hierarchy @JsonTypeInfo with an explicit subtype list, never blanket default typing.
The discriminator property name and subtype names are the wire contract; renaming a class without keeping its @JsonSubTypes name breaks every queued message.
Records need jackson-databind 2.12+ (with parameter names) to deserialise; the older bean-style requirement is a silent failure mode for mixed-version producers.

variants.name: JDK serialisation + JMS ObjectMessage / RMI (classic form)
variants.implementation_notes: The platform's original answer: `implements Serializable` on the command, `ObjectOutputStream`/RMI or a JMS ObjectMessage to ship it, and `readObject` on the far side reconstructing the object graph before the invoker calls execute(). It is short and needs no codec code, but it is also the canonical insecure-deserialization surface: any class on the consumer's classpath can be instantiated from a crafted message, so this variant belongs behind an authenticated broker with a single trusted producer, or in a migration path toward a JSON/protobuf envelope.
pitfalls: Deserialising untrusted bytes executes gadgets: JMS ObjectMessage plus a message converter that trusts a typeId header is a documented CVE class.
serialVersionUID drift and class evolution produce InvalidClassException on messages that are already in the queue; serialisation also bypasses constructors, so invariants never hold.
The serialised graph is far larger than the data it carries - sending a command that references other objects drags them along.

variants.name: Sealed interface + records with a pattern-matching switch dispatcher
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface Command + records + exhaustive switch
variants.implementation_notes: Modern Java closes the hierarchy instead of registering it: a `sealed interface Command permits ...` with one record per command makes the set known to the compiler, and the invoker is a `switch` over the sealed type with pattern matching - exhaustiveness is checked, no registry and no reflection. Jackson (2.15+) or a protobuf oneof can still produce the wire envelope, and records give correct equals/hashCode for free, which matters when commands are de-duplicated on the queue.
pitfalls: A sealed set is closed per package/module: a command added elsewhere cannot be deserialised through the base type without reopening the hierarchy.
Jackson needs the sealed subtype list (or @JsonSubTypes) to map the discriminator onto the permitted records; deriving it from the payload's class name reintroduces the gadget risk.
Java 21 is required for pattern matching in switch after the preview cycle - pin the toolchain or keep an if/else instanceof chain for older runtimes.
